title: The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond
venue: Foundations and Trends in Information Retrieval
abstract: This survey derives the BM25 ranking function from the probabilistic relevance framework and analyses its two central components: term frequency saturation and document length normalization. It then shows how the same framework extends to field weighting, relevance feedback and pseudo relevance feedback, and discusses the parameter sensitivity that practitioners observe in ad hoc retrieval experiments.

title: Okapi at TREC-3
abstract: The Okapi system took part in the routing and ad hoc retrieval tasks of TREC-3 using a probabilistic term weighting scheme with explicit term frequency and document length components. The paper reports the parameter settings that later became the standard BM25 configuration and studies how relevance feedback changes retrieval effectiveness on the same collection.

title: A Language Modeling Approach to Information Retrieval
abstract: This paper proposes treating a user query as a sample generated from a document language model, so that documents are ranked by the likelihood of producing the query. The formulation removes the need for ad hoc term weighting heuristics and provides a principled place for smoothing, which controls how much probability mass is reserved for unseen query terms.

title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
abstract: The authors show that dense retrieval can outperform a strong sparse BM25 baseline for open-domain question answering when the retriever is trained on a modest number of question-passage pairs. A simple dual encoder architecture is optimized with an in-batch negative sampling objective and then combined with a reader model for end-to-end answer extraction.

title: ColBERT: Efficient and Effective Passage Search via Contextualized Late Interaction over BERT
abstract: ColBERT introduces a late interaction architecture that encodes queries and passages independently with BERT and scores them with a MaxSim operator over token level embeddings. This keeps the expressiveness of contextualized representations while allowing offline indexing and fast passage search, narrowing the gap between effectiveness and latency.

title: Learning to Rank for Information Retrieval
venue: Foundations and Trends in Information Retrieval
abstract: This survey formulates retrieval as a supervised machine learning problem over query document feature vectors and reviews pointwise, pairwise and listwise learning to rank approaches. It discusses evaluation measures such as NDCG and MAP, the construction of labeled training data, and the trade-off between ranking accuracy and inference cost.

title: Query Expansion Using Local and Global Document Analysis
abstract: The paper compares local and global techniques for query expansion, where expansion terms are selected from top ranked documents or from a collection wide association thesaurus. Experiments show that local analysis driven by pseudo relevance feedback gives consistent gains over the original query, while global analysis helps mainly for short queries.

title: Efficient and Robust Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search Using Hierarchical Navigable Small World Graphs
abstract: The authors present a hierarchical graph structure for approximate nearest neighbor search in high dimensional vector spaces. The index is built incrementally, supports logarithmic search complexity, and remains accurate for embeddings used in dense retrieval and recommendation, making it a standard backend for vector databases.

title: The PageRank Citation Ranking: Bringing Order to the Web
abstract: PageRank interprets a hyperlink as a vote and computes a stationary distribution of a random walk over the web graph, so that a page inherits importance from the pages that cite it. The paper relates this citation ranking to academic bibliometrics and describes how the score can be combined with text similarity for web search.

title: Indexing by Latent Semantic Analysis
venue: Journal of the American Society for Information Science
abstract: Latent semantic analysis applies truncated singular value decomposition to a term document matrix and retrieves in the resulting low dimensional space. Because the projection groups terms that co-occur, the method partially solves the synonymy problem of exact term matching and improves retrieval when queries and documents use different vocabulary.

title: BEIR: A Heterogeneous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models
abstract: BEIR collects eighteen retrieval datasets across domains and tasks and evaluates models in a zero-shot setting. The study finds that sparse BM25 remains a surprisingly strong and robust baseline, while dense retrievers trained on one domain often generalize poorly, which motivates research on domain transfer and hybrid retrieval.

title: Attention Is All You Need
abstract: The Transformer replaces recurrence and convolution with stacked self-attention layers and a position-wise feed-forward network, allowing sequence to sequence translation to be trained in parallel over all positions. Multi-head attention lets the model attend to information from different representation subspaces, and the architecture becomes the backbone of later pretrained language models.

title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
abstract: BERT pretrains a deep bidirectional Transformer with a masked language modeling objective and a next sentence prediction task, then fine-tunes the same encoder for downstream tasks with a small task specific head. The pretrain then fine-tune paradigm removes much of the need for task specific architecture engineering and sets new results on eleven language understanding benchmarks.

title: Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space
abstract: This paper introduces two log-linear models, continuous bag of words and skip-gram, that learn distributed word embeddings from large unlabeled corpora at low computational cost. The learned vectors capture semantic and syntactic regularities, so that simple vector arithmetic such as analogy questions becomes possible in the embedding space.

title: GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation
abstract: GloVe trains word embeddings by factorizing a global word-word co-occurrence matrix with a weighted least squares objective. Combining global corpus statistics with local context windows gives pretrained vectors that perform well on word similarity, analogy and named entity recognition tasks.

title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
abstract: The authors train a 175 billion parameter autoregressive language model and evaluate it without gradient updates, providing only a handful of demonstrations in the prompt. Performance improves smoothly with model size, and many tasks that previously required supervised fine-tuning become solvable through in-context learning alone.

title: Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer
abstract: T5 casts every text problem, including classification and translation, into a text-to-text format so that a single encoder-decoder model and a single training objective cover all tasks. The paper systematically compares pretraining objectives, architectures and datasets, and releases the cleaned C4 corpus used for training.

title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
abstract: The paper adds an attention mechanism to an encoder-decoder translation model so that the decoder searches for the relevant part of the source sentence at each step instead of relying on a single fixed length vector. The soft alignment learned by attention improves translation quality, especially for long sentences, and becomes the conceptual basis of later self-attention models.

title: Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks
abstract: Sentence-BERT fine-tunes a Siamese BERT network so that semantically similar sentences receive close sentence embeddings, reducing the cost of pairwise similarity search from quadratic to linear. The resulting bi-encoder supports semantic similarity, clustering and semantic search with a cosine similarity index over fixed length vectors.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
abstract: RAG couples a dense retriever over a Wikipedia index with a sequence-to-sequence generator, conditioning each answer on retrieved passages instead of relying only on parameters. The hybrid approach produces more specific and factual text than a comparable closed book generator and allows the knowledge source to be updated without retraining.

title: A Conditional Random Field Word Segmenter for Chinese Word Segmentation
abstract: The paper treats Chinese word segmentation as a character level sequence labeling problem and applies a conditional random field with character identity, n-gram and dictionary features. It reports strong accuracy across four SIGHAN bakeoff corpora and shows that segmentation quality directly affects downstream retrieval and parsing.

title: Long Short-Term Memory
abstract: Long short-term memory introduces a memory cell controlled by input, forget and output gates, which lets a recurrent network preserve information over long time lags. The architecture mitigates the vanishing gradient problem of plain recurrent networks and becomes the dominant sequence model before attention based architectures.

title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
abstract: Residual learning reformulates a stack of layers as learning a residual mapping with a shortcut connection, which makes very deep convolutional networks trainable. A 152 layer ResNet wins the ImageNet classification challenge and the identity shortcuts are later reused in nearly every deep vision and language model.

title: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
abstract: AlexNet trains a large convolutional neural network on the ImageNet classification dataset using two GPUs, rectified linear units and dropout regularization. The model cuts the top-5 error rate far below previous hand engineered features and marks the point where deep learning replaced classical computer vision pipelines.

title: You Only Look Once: Unified, Real-Time Object Detection
abstract: YOLO frames object detection as a single regression problem that predicts bounding boxes and class probabilities directly from the full image in one network pass. Because it reasons about the image globally, the detector runs at real time frame rates and makes far fewer background false positives than region proposal based pipelines.

title: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale
abstract: The Vision Transformer splits an image into fixed size patches, embeds each patch as a token and applies a standard Transformer encoder for classification. Given sufficient pretraining data the architecture matches or exceeds convolutional networks, showing that image specific inductive biases are not strictly necessary.

title: Mask R-CNN
abstract: Mask R-CNN adds a mask prediction branch to Faster R-CNN and replaces coarse region pooling with a pixel accurate RoIAlign operator. The simple extension trains instance segmentation, object detection and keypoint estimation jointly and becomes a standard baseline for dense visual recognition.

title: Generative Adversarial Networks
abstract: A generative adversarial network trains a generator and a discriminator in a minimax game, where the generator learns to produce samples that the discriminator cannot distinguish from real data. The framework generates sharp images without an explicit likelihood and becomes the dominant approach to image synthesis before diffusion models.

title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models
abstract: This paper connects diffusion probabilistic models to denoising score matching and shows that a simple training objective predicting the added noise yields high quality image generation. Sampling progressively denoises Gaussian noise, and the formulation later underpins text-to-image systems and diffusion based video generation.

title: Segment Anything
abstract: Segment Anything introduces a promptable segmentation model trained on a billion masks collected through a data engine loop. The model transfers zero-shot to unseen image distributions given point, box or text prompts, establishing a foundation model for segmentation similar to what large language models provide for text.

title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis
abstract: NeRF encodes a scene as a multilayer perceptron that maps a 3D coordinate and viewing direction to density and color, then renders images with differentiable volume rendering. Optimizing the network on a set of posed images produces photorealistic novel views and inspires a large family of neural 3D reconstruction methods.

title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization
abstract: Adam combines momentum with per parameter scaling of the learning rate by estimates of the first and second moments of the gradients. The update requires little tuning, handles sparse gradients well, and becomes the default optimizer for training deep networks and large language models.

title: Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting
abstract: Dropout randomly removes units during training so that the network cannot rely on any single feature pathway, which acts as a strong regularizer against overfitting. At test time the weights are scaled to approximate an ensemble of exponentially many thinned networks, and the technique substantially improves generalization on vision and speech tasks.

title: Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift
abstract: Batch normalization normalizes layer inputs using mini-batch statistics and learns a scale and shift parameter for each activation. The technique allows much higher learning rates, reduces sensitivity to initialization and acts as a mild regularizer, which shortens training time for deep convolutional networks considerably.

title: XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System
abstract: XGBoost presents a regularized objective for gradient boosted trees together with a sparsity aware split finding algorithm and a weighted quantile sketch for approximate learning. The system scales to billions of examples on a single machine and dominates structured data competitions and industrial ranking pipelines.

title: Random Forests
abstract: Random forests grow many decision trees on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets at each split and average their predictions. The ensemble reduces variance without increasing bias, provides out-of-bag error estimates and internal feature importance, and remains a strong baseline for tabular classification and regression.

title: A Survey on Contrastive Self-supervised Learning
abstract: This survey organizes contrastive self-supervised learning around three design choices: how positive and negative pairs are constructed, how the encoder is trained, and how representations are evaluated. It compares pretext tasks across vision and language, and discusses how contrastive pretraining reduces the dependence on labeled data.

title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
abstract: The authors measure how cross entropy loss of a language model depends on parameter count, dataset size and compute, and find smooth power law relationships over many orders of magnitude. The empirical laws allow practitioners to predict the loss of a larger model and to allocate a fixed compute budget between model size and training tokens.

title: Learning Representations by Back-Propagating Errors
abstract: This paper popularizes the backpropagation algorithm for computing gradients of a multi-layer network by applying the chain rule backwards through the layers. It shows that hidden layers learn useful internal representations, resolving the credit assignment problem that had limited earlier perceptron models.

title: A Tutorial on Spectral Clustering
abstract: This tutorial explains spectral clustering as a relaxation of the graph partitioning problem using the eigenvectors of a graph Laplacian. It compares normalized and unnormalized variants, discusses the choice of similarity graph and number of clusters, and clarifies when the method outperforms k-means on non-convex data.

title: MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters
abstract: MapReduce expresses a computation as a map function over key-value pairs followed by a reduce function that aggregates by key, and the runtime handles partitioning, scheduling and fault recovery. The abstraction hides the complexity of parallel processing on commodity clusters and enables large scale log and index building pipelines.

title: The Google File System
abstract: The Google File System stores data in large chunks replicated across commodity machines, with a single master holding metadata and lease based coordination for mutations. The design tolerates frequent component failures, optimizes for append heavy workloads, and provides the storage substrate for later batch processing frameworks.

title: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store
abstract: Dynamo combines consistent hashing, vector clocks and tunable quorum reads and writes to provide an always writable key-value store on top of unreliable machines. The paper argues that availability can take priority over strong consistency for shopping cart workloads, and popularizes the eventual consistency model in industrial storage systems.

title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm
abstract: Raft decomposes consensus into leader election, log replication and safety, and uses randomized timeouts and a strong leader to keep the protocol understandable. The design provides the same guarantees as Paxos with a clearer structure, and it has been adopted by many production systems for replicated state machines.

title: Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database
abstract: Spanner shards data across datacenters and uses synchronized clocks with bounded uncertainty, exposed as TrueTime, to assign commit timestamps and enforce external consistency. The system supports globally distributed transactions with strong serializability at scale, showing that wide area consistency is achievable with careful hardware support.

title: Ray: A Distributed Framework for Emerging AI Applications
abstract: Ray provides a unified programming model with stateless tasks and stateful actors, backed by a distributed scheduler and an in-memory object store. The runtime targets the fine grained, heterogeneous workloads of reinforcement learning and model serving, achieving low task latency and high throughput on large clusters.

title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
abstract: PagedAttention stores the key-value cache of a large language model in non-contiguous blocks inspired by virtual memory paging, which nearly eliminates memory fragmentation during serving. The vLLM system built on this idea improves serving throughput by an order of magnitude at the same latency, making efficient inference a systems problem rather than only a modeling one.

title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
abstract: FlashAttention computes exact attention with a tiling strategy that keeps intermediate blocks in on-chip memory and avoids materializing the full attention matrix in high bandwidth memory. The IO aware kernel speeds up training and inference of Transformer models and enables much longer context windows at reduced memory cost.

title: Efficient Transformers: A Survey
abstract: This survey categorizes efficient Transformer variants into sparse attention, low rank approximations, kernel methods and recurrent reformulations, comparing their asymptotic complexity and empirical trade-offs. It argues that quadratic self-attention is the main bottleneck for long sequences and that no single family dominates across tasks.

title: Pre-train, Prompt, and Predict: A Systematic Survey of Prompting Methods in Natural Language Processing
abstract: This survey reframes NLP tasks as cloze style language modeling problems solved by prompts, and organizes the field into prompt templates, answer engineering and answer-verbalizer mapping. It reviews prompt based fine-tuning and zero-shot prompting, and discusses the gap between small supervised models and large pretrained models used through in-context learning.
